title: Deferred execution
summary: A LINQ query is a recipe, not a result. Learn when it actually runs, and write your own lazy sequences with yield.

steps.title: A query is a recipe
body: This line does **not** filter anything yet:
```csharp
var overdue = invoices.Where(i => i.DaysLate > 0);

It builds an `IEnumerable<Invoice>`: an object that *knows how* to produce the overdue invoices. The filtering happens later, when something asks for the items: a `foreach`, a `ToList()`, a `Count()`.
This is called **deferred execution**, or being **lazy**. `Where`, `Select`, `OrderBy`, `Take` and `Skip` are all lazy.
Why build it that way?
- You can add steps to a query in several places before any work is done.
- Work that is never needed is never done. `query.First()` stops at the first match.
One consequence surprises everyone once: the query reads the source **at the moment it runs**, so it sees changes made after the query was written.

steps.explain: `big` is only a recipe. It runs when `Count()` is called, and by then the list holds 1, 2, 3, 10. Three of those are greater than 1.
Nothing ever asks `lengths` for its items, so the lambda never runs. A query that is never enumerated does no work at all.

steps.title: Run once: ToList
body: A lazy query has no memory. **Every time** you enumerate it, it runs again from the start.
```csharp
var valid = readings.Where(r => IsValid(r));   // IsValid is slow
int count = valid.Count();   // runs the whole filter
int max   = valid.Max();     // runs the whole filter again
If the source is a database query or a file, that means the database is queried twice or the file is read twice.
`ToList()` (or `ToArray()`) runs the query **once, now** and stores the results. This is called **materialising**.
```csharp
var valid = readings.Where(r => IsValid(r)).ToList();   // runs here, once
int count = valid.Count;     // just reads the list
int max   = valid.Max();     // just reads the list
Rule of thumb: if you will use the results more than once, materialise them. A materialised list is also a snapshot: later changes to the source do not affect it.

steps.prompt: `calls` counts how often the lambda runs. What does this print?
code: var doubled = new[] { 1, 2, 3 }.Select(n => { calls++; return n * 2; });
steps.explain: `Sum` and `Max` each run the query over all three items: 6 calls. `ToList` runs it one more time: 9. After that, `list.Sum()` and `list.Max()` read the stored values and the lambda is not called again.

steps.prompt: Which calls only build a recipe, and which ones run the query right away?
steps.explain: A quick test: if the method returns another sequence (`IEnumerable<T>`), it is lazy. If it returns a finished value or collection, it had to run the query to get it.

steps.title: Read the sensor once
prompt: `Summary` reports on sensor readings. Negative readings are faults and are ignored.
The text is right, but reading the sensor is slow and this code reads **all of it three times**. Change it so the source is enumerated only **once**. The tests count.
template: Dojo.Eq("Summary text is still right", "3 valid, min 2, max 9", Summary(Sensor()));
Dojo.Eq("the sensor was read exactly once", 1, passes);
Dojo.Eq("Summary works on a plain list", "2 valid, min 5, max 6", Summary(new List<int> { 5, -3, 6 }));
hints: `valid` is a lazy query. `Count()`, `Min()` and `Max()` each run it from the start, and each run reads `readings` again.
Materialise the query once, then ask the stored results three questions.
Add `.ToList()` to the end of the `Where` line. Nothing else has to change.

steps.title: yield return
body: You can write your own lazy sequence. A method that returns `IEnumerable<T>` and uses **`yield return`** is called an **iterator**.
```csharp
static IEnumerable<int> Countdown(int from)
for (int i = from; i >= 1; i--)
yield return i;
foreach (int n in Countdown(3))
Console.WriteLine(n);   // 3, 2, 1
It does not build a list. It hands out **one item at a time**:
1. Calling `Countdown(3)` runs *none* of the body. It returns a recipe.
2. When the `foreach` asks for an item, the body runs until it hits `yield return`. That value goes to the caller and the method **pauses** right there.
3. When the next item is asked for, the method **resumes** after the `yield return`, with all its local variables intact.
4. When the body ends (or reaches `yield break;`), the sequence is finished.
`Where` and `Select` are written exactly this way.

steps.prompt: Arrange the lines into an iterator that yields `from`, then each number down to 1, and finally 0.
steps.explain: The loop yields `from` down to 1, pausing at each one. Only after the loop has finished does the method reach `yield return 0;`.

steps.prompt: The iterator and the loop take turns. What does this print?
steps.explain: The iterator runs to the first `yield return` and pauses; the loop body prints `got 1`. Asking for the next item resumes the iterator, which prints `middle` and yields 2. Asking once more runs it to the end.

steps.title: Infinite sequences
body: Because an iterator only produces what is asked for, it is allowed to **never end**.
```csharp
static IEnumerable<int> Naturals()
int n = 1;
while (true)
yield return n++;
var firstFive   = Naturals().Take(5);                          // 1 2 3 4 5
var threeSquares = Naturals().Select(n => n * n).Take(3);     // 1 4 9
The `while (true)` is safe because the loop pauses at every `yield return`, and `Take(5)` stops asking after five items.
> **Tip:** Never call `ToList()`, `Count()` or `OrderBy` directly on an infinite sequence. They need *every* item, so they never finish. Limit it first with `Take` or `First`.

steps.title: Your own lazy operators
prompt: - `static IEnumerable<T> TakeUntil<T>(IEnumerable<T> source, Func<T, bool> stop)`
Yields items from `source` one by one. The first time `stop(item)` is `true`, it ends **without** yielding that item.
`TakeUntil` must be lazy too: it has to work on an infinite source.
starter: static IEnumerable<T> TakeUntil<T>(IEnumerable<T> source, Func<T, bool> stop)
// yield each item until stop(item) says true
solution: static IEnumerable<T> TakeUntil<T>(IEnumerable<T> source, Func<T, bool> stop)
template: Dojo.Eq<IEnumerable<int>>("TakeUntil(Multiples(6), n => n > 20) is 6, 12, 18", new[] { 6, 12, 18 }, TakeUntil(Multiples(6), n => n > 20).ToList());
Dojo.Eq<IEnumerable<string>>("TakeUntil stops at the first ERROR line", new[] { "start", "load" }, TakeUntil(new List<string> { "start", "load", "ERROR", "save" }, s => s == "ERROR").ToList());
Dojo.Eq<IEnumerable<int>>("TakeUntil yields everything when stop is never true", new[] { 1, 2, 3 }, TakeUntil(new[] { 1, 2, 3 }, n => n > 99).ToList());
for (int i = 1; ; i++) { pulled++; yield return i; }
Dojo.Check("TakeUntil is lazy: it pulls only what is asked for", firstTwo.Count == 2 && pulled <= 3, $"taking 2 items pulled {pulled} items from the source");

forbid.message: Does not call the built-in TakeWhile

hints: `Multiples`: keep a variable that starts at `of`. Inside `while (true)`, `yield return` it, then add `of` to it.
`if (stop(item)) yield break;` ends the sequence. Otherwise `yield return item;`.
